profiles.name: Chippewa
remainingGaps: Broaden community-specific readings beyond these Michigan and Minnesota examples and keep named governments distinct.
The dictionary’s older speaker figures and the Sault page’s dated program descriptions are not current censuses or a program audit.

This alternate-name route does not create another nation alongside Ojibwe or make Anishinaabe identity universal. The pictured artist’s individual name and community are unrecorded; no design meanings or endorsement are inferred.

profiles.name: Ojibwe
remainingGaps: The seven Minnesota governments have not all received equally deep, direct source review. Leech Lake now has a Band-published historical overview and two reported court opinions, but the underlying treaty texts, 1973 settlement document, current rules, and later legal history still need review; Fond du Lac needs more direct public history and treaty material; separate institutional and community voices should be deepened for every Band and Red Lake Nation.

The Minnesota Chippewa Tribe website’s linked History of the Tribe page did not expose substantive text through the inspection tool, and the direct 2015 Leech Lake annual report exceeded the source tool’s document-size limit. The Leech Lake Band’s historical overview and the full reported opinions in Leech Lake Band v. Herbst (1971) and State v. Forge (1977) were inspected; the booklet’s later MOU, appendices, implementation materials, underlying treaties, and settlement document were not independently reviewed.

The full Bois Forte oral-history transcripts listed by its museum, the Smithsonian video transcript, and the Mille Lacs Band’s linked Social History book were not read. They are not represented as inspected sources.

Specialist Ojibwe language scholarship, treaty originals and legal decisions, more community-authored records from Grand Portage, White Earth and Red Lake, and relevant communities in Wisconsin and Canada remain to be reviewed.

The Minnesota Indian Affairs Council’s older Fond du Lac sketch includes broad, dated ethnographic descriptions; it is retained only as supporting context and those generalizations are not carried into the synthesis.
No Ojibwe community review or endorsement is recorded.

profiles.name: Anishinaabe
remainingGaps: Broaden direct community histories and Indigenous scholarship beyond the selected Great Lakes and Ontario examples; these institutions do not represent all Anishinaabe peoples.

Investigate additional Algonquin, Saulteaux and other community-specific uses of related identities through their own sources; shared names do not justify automatic affiliation or interchangeable language labels.
Review current constitutional ratifiers/amendments, education-system participants and project outcomes separately. Reported approvals and activities are not independent outcome evaluations.

The full Odawa/Eastern Ojibwe dictionary, GLIFWC treaty guide,2023 vulnerability assessment and finished food cookbook remain unread leads. No recordings were listened to and no map/media reuse licence is inferred.

Keep differing Three Fires interpretations attributed. No universal duty chart, precise migration timetable, current population/speaker count, individual harvesting eligibility or restricted cultural instructions is supplied. Community review remains open.

profiles.name: Ottawa (Odawa)

Original Odawa Area Scouting link is retained as an unassessed lead; Indigenous authorship and direct community-history scope have not been established. It is excluded from the curated guide.
No present population, enrollment, border, legal-rights or treaty-implementation conclusion follows from these readings. No community review or endorsement is recorded.

profiles.name: Wyandot

The Ohio bowl image is precisely identified related Wendat/Huron material culture. Its maker and particular community are unrecorded; it does not depict a particular Wyandot government.

The shared 1843 Amiskquew portrait gives historical Menominee context, not a depiction of the contemporary government or its present officeholders.

profiles.name: Ho-Chunk Nation
remainingGaps: Add Ho-Chunk-authored historical scholarship, public family accounts and removal/return histories beyond these brief institutional descriptions.
Read current constitutions, amendments and laws before making precise legal, jurisdictional or governmental-process claims.
The wider Ho-Chunk people and the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska require their own scoped histories; this named Wisconsin government is not interchangeable with either wider label or another government.
Current language access, fluency and program outcomes were not evaluated; internal records and restricted cultural information remain outside this public starting path.
The photograph documents Marlon WhiteEagle’s office in May2021 only; no current officeholder or endorsement is implied.
